label: resolve_tradeoff
rationale: TokenList.__init__ calls super().__init__(None, str(self)), which flattens and joins every child value at construction; group_tokens therefore pays an O(group size) join for every group created, and Statement() pays it for every statement. Make value (and normalized, which equals value for groups) a lazily-evaluated property on TokenList: store a sentinel at construction and compute ''.join of the flattened values on first access, also replacing the eager 'grp.value = str(start)' in the extend p

ath with invalidation.
Why it should win: Every call to group_tokens from _group (72k calls) and _group_matching (9.8k calls) constructs or extends a TokenList, each time re-joining the full subtree text; flatten alone shows 743k calls (3.5%). Most group values are never read before the group is re-wrapped into a larger group, so the joins are wasted. Statement construction in the splitter does the same full join per statement. Deferring the join eliminates the quadratic build-up.
Precondition:

Grouping only restructures the tree; it never changes the concatenated flattened text, so a value computed lazily at first read equals the value computed eagerly at construction. Any mutation that does change text (reindent filter insertions) must invalidate the cache, or filters must read via str(), which already recomputes. TokenList uses __slots__, so a cached slot plus a property override is possible.
Why the output stays the same: For groups, value is only consumed via str(), .value reads a

nd match()/normalized. Because regrouping preserves the flattened character sequence, the lazily computed string is character-for-character the eager one at every read point; where text does change (whitespace insertion), the cache is invalidated so reads recompute, matching current str() behaviour. Output is byte-identical.
title: Compute TokenList.value lazily to avoid O(n²) string joins during grouping

label: name_the_problem
rationale:
In process, replace per-token tuple membership tests and the T.Keyword containment check with identity checks against a precomputed frozenset of whitespace and comment types, and for non-keyword, non-punctuation tokens, skip _change_splitlevel entirely. Hoist the module attribute lookups (T.Punctuation, T.Keyword, T.Whitespace) into locals before the loop.
Why it should win: A token-stream state machine runs on all tokens, 801 calls but 13% self-time. Each token goes through a method call and se

veral tuple-containment tests that call the _TokenType.__contains__ method (498k calls, 4%). A set lookup by identity is a standard scanner fast-path.
Precondition: Token types are singleton _TokenType objects. A non-Keyword, non-Punctuation ttype always yields 0 from _change_splitlevel; keyword subtype membership is the same as the existing 'in T.Keyword' check.
Why the output stays the same: The skipped calls would return 0 and mutate no state; the remaining branches are evaluated with the sam
e conditions, so statement boundaries are identical.
title: Statement splitter: precomputed keyword-type fast reject and skip Token double construction work

label: name_the_problem
rationale:
Rewrite TokenList.flatten so it walks the token tree with an explicit stack of child iterators held in a local list, yielding leaf tokens in the same depth-first left-to-right order. This removes the per-level generator creation and the chained yield-from delegation that every leaf currently passes through.
Why it should win: flatten has 743244 calls and about 3.5 percent self time, and it is the recursive generator used by __str__ on every group, so each Statement and nested group string rebuil

ds through many delegating generators. Replacing the recursion with one loop over a stack is a standard control-flow reduction from compiler and tree-iteration practice, and it cuts generator frame overhead per leaf.
Precondition: Token trees are finite and acyclic, and no caller mutates the tree while a flatten generator is being consumed in a way that would change the traversal order. The benchmark only consumes flatten to build strings and filter leaves.
Why the output stays the same: The sta
ck traversal yields the same leaf tokens in the same order as the recursive version, so ''.join of the values and every consumer see identical data and the output bytes are unchanged.
title: Flatten TokenList via an explicit stack instead of nested recursive generators in sql.py

label: resolve_tradeoff
rationale: Rewrite _windowed_running_min and _windowed_running_max to process the input in consecutive blocks of maxlen items (collected with a list/islice). For the first block yield its prefix minima (accumulate(block, min)). For every later block compute the previous block's suffix minima (accumulate over reversed block, then reversed back) and the current block's prefix minima, and yield map(min, prefix_cur[j], suffix_prev[j+1]) for j < len-1, plus prefix_cur[-1] for the block's last element (whole-blo

ck window). The final partial block uses the same pairing truncated to its length. Same for max.
Why it should win: Both functions are ~6% self time each (200k calls, ~12% combined) and are pure per-item Python: enumerate, two deque index checks, a while loop, tuple creation, generator resume. The block decomposition does O(1) amortised work per item like the deque, but moves all per-item work into C (accumulate, reversed, map, min) with Python overhead only once per block of maxlen items. Expec

t the two functions to fall to a fraction of their current cost.
Precondition: Trade-off: the deque keeps strict laziness (one item in, one out) at the price of ~10 Python bytecode operations per item; separating the stream by scale into maxlen-sized blocks lets each block be reduced in C. Requires values where equal elements are indistinguishable in the output (ints in the benchmark; -0.0/0.0 or NaN floats or Decimal with differing representations could print differently since tie-breaking orde

r changes) and that consuming up to maxlen items ahead of the consumer is unobservable (source not shared or side-effecting).
Why the output stays the same: The window minimum of positions [i-maxlen+1, i] equals min(suffix-min of the previous block from the window start, prefix-min of the current block up to i); for i inside the first block the window starts at 0 so the prefix-min alone is correct; when the window exactly covers a block the prefix-min of its last element is the block min. The se

quence of yielded values is therefore identical element by element for totally ordered values; on ties both versions yield a value equal to the minimum, which for ints prints identically. Output length and ordering unchanged.
title: Block-based (van Herk) sliding min/max via C-level accumulate/map instead of per-item deque loop

label: obvious
rationale:
In collapse, precompute the base-type tuple once, merging (str, bytes) with base_type when given. Add a fast check at the top of the node loop that yields immediately for int and float nodes, avoiding the isinstance calls and the try/iter(node) TypeError exception path.
Why it should win: collapse has 62k calls and 4% self time. Leaf ints reach iter(node) and raise TypeError, and exceptions are costly. The isinstance tuple is also rebuilt per node.
Precondition: Exact int or float instances are

never iterable. Subclasses are routed through the normal path.
Why the output stays the same: Non-iterable leaves are yielded in the same order as before. Exact-type checks leave iterable subclasses on the original logic.
title: Fast path for non-iterable ints in collapse using a type check

label: lane-9
rationale:
In _parse_link_href's non-block scan, first use a precompiled regex matching a maximal run of characters that are not whitespace, backslash, NUL or parentheses, and jump pos to its end. Only fall back to the existing per-character logic when the next character is one of those specials.
Why it should win: 10762 calls with 0.085s self time from a per-character Python loop with several membership tests per char. URLs are mostly plain runs, so a C-speed lexer skip (as in tokenizer generators) cuts t

he interpreter work.
Precondition: The skip class must exclude exactly ' \t\n\r\f', NUL, backslash, '(' and ')' so that all state-changing characters still go through the original loop.
Why the output stays the same: Characters in the skipped run do not change level, break, or return, and only advance pos by 1, so landing on the first special character gives the same state as the loop.
title: Fast-path _parse_link_href with a regex for plain href runs

label: obvious
rationale:
Add precompiled regexes for the common character sets (TOML_WS, TOML_WS_AND_NEWLINE, BARE_KEY_CHARS). Make skip_chars, or its hot call sites (loads, parse_key, parse_key_part, parse_key_value_pair, skip_comments_and_array_ws), use pattern.match(src, pos).end() instead of the Python while loop with try/except. Keep the generic loop only for any other character set.
Why it should win: skip_chars is called 502k times and takes 8% of self time. Most calls skip zero or one character, but each still p

ays the function call, the try block and the set-membership loop. A regex match runs in C, and inlining it at call sites removes the function-call overhead.
Precondition: TOML_WS is exactly space and tab, TOML_WS_AND_NEWLINE is those plus newline, and BARE_KEY_CHARS is a fixed ASCII set. The regex classes must match these sets exactly.
Why the output stays the same: The regex consumes the same maximal run of characters from the set, and a match of zero length returns the same pos. End of string
stops the run in both versions, so the returned position is identical.
title: Replace skip_chars per-character loop with compiled regex match for whitespace skipping
